canberra.title: ‘Bring it on’: Renewed push to save earless dragons
canberra.snippet: A landmark new plan hopes to save the earless dragon from the brink of extinction, but conservationists fear it doesn’t go far enou...
canberra.content:
One of southern Australia’s rarest (and smallest) residents: the earless dragon. Photo: James Coleman.

A landmark new plan hopes to save the earless dragon from the brink of extinction, but conservationists fear it doesn’t go far enough in protecting their homes.

The grassland earless dragon (GED) is incredibly rare and weighs around five grams.

A 2019 study revealed that four populations – at sites across Victoria, the ACT, Monaro and Bathurst – are really four separate species.

All are critically endangered or endangered.

The latest recovery plan went into effect in October for the rare reptiles and makes about 50 recommendations.

It’s hoped the plan will maintain (if not improve) genetic diversity, grow their habitat and see further survey and monitoring operations.

According to the plan, about 0.5 per cent of their temperate grassland habitat remains.

The recovery strategy identifies a “complex array” of threats facing the lizard species, including habitat loss from urban expansion, agricultural clearing and pesticide use.

“Development has resulted in fragmentation and direct loss of habitat to the built environment, seeded pastures, and crop fields,” the document outlines.

“Much of the remaining habitat has been degraded by weed invasions and excessive biomass buildup, as well as overgrazing, prolonged drought and extensive fire, and the loss of important functional groups such as invertebrates, macropods and dingos.”

But it’s the plan’s land use that concerns Friends of Grasslands advocacy convener Matt Whitting.

He questioned how useful the recovery plan would be in stopping urban development that could harm earless dragon populations.

Mr Whitting pointed to the Eastern Broadacre Area in the ACT, a land corridor being considered for development despite being near where wild populations of the Canberra dragon live.

“If we’re trying to recover this species, then we want to be able to expand the population outside of where it currently lives into areas where it could live,” Mr Whitting told Region.

“If we develop all of those areas, then we’ve got a problem.”

The recovery plan predicts the Monaro earless dragon species (Tympanocryptis Osbornei) is more widespread than currently known. Image: Supplied.

The plan calls for real-time satellite monitoring of grasslands to catch any changes, awareness campaigns to highlight legal protections for the dragons and support for land stewardship programs.

As of 2026, Canberra’s earless dragon populations are known to be in the Majura and Jerrabomberra valleys.

While the plan describes all four species as “cryptic and under-surveyed”, it has a particularly high hope for populations of the Monaro GED.

It notes there could be undiscovered members waiting to be found.

“The Monaro GED almost certainly has a larger population size and geographic range than the other three GEDs,” it states.

“Monitoring and research programs that focus on the Monaro GED offer the best opportunity to learn how to effectively manage grasslands and to implement recovery programs for all four species, including the highly fragmented Canberra GED.”

Mr Whitting said his overall view of the plan was to call it a “mixed bag”.

“There are so many other things in the plan that do look good,” he said.

“For example, taking action on weeds. … They choke grasslands. They make it impossible for dragons to see the sun, and they can’t live like that.

“To the extent that this plan will promote effective coordination and action, bring it on.”

Original Article published by Claire Sams on About Regional.

canberra.title: As Australia debates migration, Canberra targets 30 per cent more Southeast Asian students
canberra.snippet: At a time when Australia is restricting international student numbers and anti-migration protests are gaining attention, the ACT Governme...
canberra.content:
The ACT Government is targeting a 30 per cent increase in international student enrolments from Southeast Asia by 2030. Photo: Supplied

At a time when Australia is restricting international student numbers and anti-migration protests are gaining attention, the ACT Government wants to attract 30 per cent more students from Southeast Asia by 2030.

The ambition, announced by Chief Minister Andrew Barr, comes as the Federal Government seeks to control international student growth and concerns over housing affordability continue to fuel debate about migration.

More than 1350 students from ASEAN countries currently study in Canberra, contributing almost $100 million annually to the local economy. The ACT wants to attract about 400 more, particularly from Indonesia, Singapore, Vietnam and Thailand.

But the announcement raises an obvious question: how does Canberra plan to increase enrolments when the Commonwealth is managing student numbers nationally?

The Federal Government has set a national planning level of 295,000 new international student commencements for 2027, unchanged from 2026. Meanwhile, anti-migration rallies have continued across Australia, including one in Sydney on 8 November, with another planned for Canberra.

While student visas and permanent migration are different, the debate over population growth has increasingly brought international education into the spotlight.

For Canberra, the economic stakes are considerable. International education is the ACT’s largest export industry, worth $1.37 billion in 2025, supporting jobs across education, hospitality, tourism and retail.

Mr Barr said stronger ties with Southeast Asia were important for Canberra’s future.

“Growing our relationships with ASEAN is about more than student numbers. It’s about attracting talented people, building research partnerships, supporting future workforce needs and creating long-term economic links,” he said.

Asked how the ACT would achieve its target under federal restrictions, the government said it intended to increase Canberra’s share of students from priority ASEAN markets within the Commonwealth’s managed system. It said the national framework encouraged universities to build stronger links with Southeast Asia and considered student accommodation when assessing growth.

The ACT spokesperson said its target covered the total number of Southeast Asian students studying in Canberra by 2030, while federal restrictions applied to students starting new courses each year.

However, the ACT did not identify any additional student allocations secured from the Commonwealth or provide annual targets showing how the increase would be achieved.

It also rejected suggestions that attracting more Southeast Asian students would mean fewer places for students from India and China, saying both remained important markets.

The ACT is particularly interested in students studying artificial intelligence, cyber security, engineering, health and renewable energy, areas where it hopes to build its future workforce.

Mr Barr has described international students as tomorrow’s researchers, skilled workers and business leaders. But that ambition also raises questions about the relationship between education and migration.

The ACT currently receives 1600 skilled migration nomination places annually, split equally between permanent Skilled Nominated visas and Skilled Work Regional visas. The government said some international graduates would return home, while others might remain in Canberra if employment opportunities were available.

“Canberra has a strong interest in retaining skilled graduates where opportunities exist,” the spokesperson told Region.

It sees both outcomes as beneficial, through skilled workers who stay and international connections built by those who leave.

Housing, however, remains a practical concern. An additional 400 students over several years may be a relatively modest increase, but Canberra is already dealing with rental affordability pressures.

Asked whether universities would need to provide more student accommodation before expanding enrolments, the government pointed to existing purpose-built housing and broader plans to increase housing supply. It did not provide an estimate of how much additional accommodation would be needed or whether any new student housing requirements would be introduced.

The ACT says it will work with universities, CIT and industry partners to pursue the target as part of its broader trade strategy.

There is a reasonable economic case for attracting more international students. They bring revenue, support local businesses and can help fill skills shortages. But with the Commonwealth managing student growth and migration under increasing scrutiny, Canberra will need to show how its target fits within federal allocations and what it means for housing.

canberra.title: A 19-minute drive separates the ‘best’ parmi across two states, so which one is better?
canberra.snippet: Good news if you love your parmis! The best chicken parmigianas in the ACT and NSW are just 19 minutes apart. Following the close of the ...
canberra.content:
Laurence Kain, managing director of Capital Brewing Co, accepted a suite of awards at the 2026 AHA awards for the ACT. Photo: Capital Brewing Co.

Good news if you love your parmis! The best chicken parmigianas in the ACT and NSW are just 19 minutes apart.

Following the close of the Australian Hotels Association (AHA) 2026 Awards for Excellence, the top pub classics across both jurisdictions now sit just down the road from one another – with Canberra’s Lager House and Queanbeyan’s Tourist Hotel taking home the respective crowns.

In the ACT, newcomer Capital Brewing Co’s Lager House took the parmi crown along with a swag of awards for their combined businesses, including best new venue, best sustainability and environment practices, best draught beer quality, best steak and best event concept and delivery.

Managing director Laurence Kain, who was also inducted into the AHA Hall of Fame at the awards ceremony, took to LinkedIn to thank his ‘superstar’ operations team, joking that from the long list of awards, the best parmi was arguably the most important.

Sally Bridgford (left) and chef Suresh Upreti (middle) accepted the best parmi award alongside Matthew Keys from event sponsor Konami. Photo: The Tourist Hotel.

Just over the border, Queanbeyan’s Tourist Hotel, a historic pub built in 1932, won the New South Wales best parmi title at an awards ceremony at Royal Randwick Racecourse.

Licensee Sally Bridgford was thrilled with the win and proud of the team working with head chef Suresh Upreti.

“To take home the win at the AHA awards for best Parmi is a great achievement for us here at The Tourist Hotel. All pubs do a Parmi, and to know ours is the top pick, it’s outstanding and a true testament to the hard work from our chefs,” Sally told Region.

With two winners sitting almost side by side, the question is: what makes a great parmi?

The Tourist Hotel Parmi can be snapped up for as little as $24 on specials nights. Photo: Tenele Conway.

Chef Upreti from The Tourist Hotel said it’s all about quality and consistency.

“The secret to a great parmi comes down to consistency, quality ingredients and taking pride in what we serve,” he explained.

“We use our own house-made seasoning to achieve a delicious flavour and crispy texture. We top our schnitzels with our house-made Napoli sauce and mozzarella cheese, then finish them in a high-temperature oven to achieve that beautiful golden colour on top.”

If you break down the parmis (literally and metaphysically), the offering is quite different.

Country pubs offering parmis are a dime a dozen in Queanbeyan, and that keeps prices low.

Time your visit to The Tourist Hotel on a Monday, and you’ll land a parmi on the ‘free toppers’ special for $25.

Come on a Wednesday when the schnitzel itself drops in price, and you’ll save another dollar on the parmi.

On every other night of the week, you’re in for a reasonable $29.

For this, you’ll get a thick chicken breast with a crunchy coating, topped with Napoli sauce, shredded double-smoked ham and a thick but not claggy or greasy layer of mozzarella.

The chips are crispy and well-seasoned, the salad is well-dressed, and the dunking sauces are punchy. All round, it’s a solid pub parmi at a good price.

The Lager House parmi comes in with bacon at $36. Photo: Tenele Conway.

Down the road, 19 minutes to be exact, at the Lager House, the parmi is $32 with the caveat that bacon is an additional $4.

While technically still a parmi without bacon, I’ve always felt it’s a must; if you feel the same as me, you’re in for a $36 parmi.

The parmi here veers a little from a classic pub parmi. You’ll still get a juicy, thick piece of crunchy chicken; the tomato-based sauce is smooth and sweet, and the bacon is well cooked, adding texture and extra crunch. The biggest departure from the classic pub parmi is that the cheese is freshly grated, not melted.

You can’t deny, it’s a very good parmi.

So you have two parmis, two approaches and two matching awards.

If you’re still left wondering which venue you should head to for the best parmi, don’t stress; they’re only 19 minutes apart. Try both, and decide for yourself.

The Tourist Hotel is located at 31 Monaro Street, Queanbeyan. They’re open 7 days a week from 10 am until late. Parking and access are at the rear while Monaro Street is under construction.

Lager House by Capital Brewing Co is located in East Traders Hall at 62 Constitution Avenue, Campbell. They’re open 7 days a week from 11:30 am until late.

canberra.title: Dogs changed Ina’s life, now she’s helping Canberra women share similar stories of their own
canberra.snippet: On a rocky outcrop of Sólheimajökull Glacier, Ina Jalil lies in black volcanic ash to capture the striking sight of Siberian Huskies as t...
canberra.content:
In 2023, a year after launching her pet photography business, Ina Jalil attended a retreat in Iceland to learn from internationally acclaimed practitioners. Photos: Supplied.

On a rocky outcrop of Sólheimajökull Glacier, Ina Jalil lies in black volcanic ash to capture the striking sight of Siberian Huskies as they splash, dig and explore.

It’s an eye-catching environment and a passionate pursuit — a world away from her previous life.

Ina first picked up a camera while completing her Bachelor of Commerce degree at the Australian National University, using photography as a creative outlet while working towards becoming an accountant or business analyst.

After graduation, Ina carved out a career in finance, while her photography developed from hobby to “side hustle”.

“I did everything — families, newborns, maternity, weddings — but I didn’t know how to run a business, so I never made much money,” she says.

“I didn’t think I could make a career out of it.”

It wasn’t until much later that she seriously considered pursuing photography as a business, prompted by an unlikely muse: her dog, Mac.

When Mac was diagnosed with heart failure at seven years old, it rocked Ina’s world.

“He was a special dog,” she says tearfully. “They told me he had six months to live, but he fought for two years.

“When Mac first got sick, I was looking for a photographer because I had taken some really nice photos of him, but I didn’t have many photos with him.”

Although a few studios were available, Ina says she couldn’t find what she was looking for.

“He loved being outdoors,” she says. ”He loved running, and I wanted to capture that personality.”

That experience influenced her own approach when, two years later, she quit her full-time EL1 role in the public service to pursue pet photography.

“It was the most terrifying thing I did,” she says.

“I didn’t tell my parents until four weeks after, because I knew if I did, they would have said, ‘What are you doing?’

“Because you’re leaving a guaranteed annual salary and secure superannuation for something you don’t know if it’s going to work.”

But the move wasn’t without planning.

“I invested in myself,” she says.

“I didn’t have the money to invest, but I knew I had to do it, so I hired a business coach and went on a payment plan, and I made the money back within one and a half months.”

Photo: Supplied.

Photo: Supplied.

Photo: Supplied.

It’s an investment that continues to pay off.

Ina won the Portrait People’s Choice category in the 2022 Asia Pacific Photography Awards. She is a Sony brand advocate, has attended international pet photography retreats, and now coaches other pet photographers around the world.

Her latest project, Barking Beautiful, will feature 28 Canberra women with their furry besties along with stories that speak to the impact of their companionship.

“I’ve sat with so many women at their ordering appointments who cried and then told me what their dog got them through,” she says.

“Stories they don’t tell many people. What surprised me was how much the answers had in common once they were all in front of me.”

Ina says mental health was a recurring theme, one she relates to personally.

When her “high-stress” financial roles led to serious mental health issues, Ina says her dogs were a huge source of support when even her friends weren’t aware of her struggles.

“The only way I got through was because of my dogs,” she says. “And that’s a common story.

“Your dog is always there no matter what happens. They don’t care how you look or how you feel. They give you unconditional love.”

One duo featured in the project is Jeannine and Beau.

Beau, a 13-year-old Bichon Frise x Poodle, first came into Jeannine’s life as a companion for her mother, who had been diagnosed with breast cancer, and Jeannine says the bond was immediate.

“I can definitely remember my mum saying to his breeder that he’s taken to me quite instantly.”

When Jeannine’s mum died in 2020 after a 10-year battle, Beau became — as her husband puts it — Jeannine’s “little shadow”.

He is also a bit of a hero.

One day out gardening in her sprawling Royalla backyard, Jeannine says her connection with Beau saved her from disaster.

Once her mother’s dog, Beau has become Jeannine’s “little shadow” and source of strength since her mum died.

“I just happened to look over at Beau and I instantly knew just by looking at him that something was wrong,” she says.

Casting her eye around, Jeannine spotted “a lovely big brown snake” just metres from her.

“If I hadn’t noticed it, we probably would have gone straight into each other.”

While clearly a loyal companion and protective pal, Beau also has healing powers.

“He is obviously that reminder and bridge to my Mum, but he has also just been this constant strength,” she says. ”It doesn’t matter what sort of day I’ve had, whether I’m a sort of tornado and really cranky, or joyously happy, his attitude towards me doesn’t change.

“We’ve been through a lot together.”

Limited places are still available for participation in Barking Beautiful. Click here for more information.

canberra.title: Gundagai Lamb adds export crown to global menu
canberra.snippet: From Old Mates Pub in Manhattan to Blue by Alain Ducasse in Bangkok, Gundagai Lamb has taken Riverina lamb onto international menus and a...
canberra.content:
Gundagai Lamb, raised in the Riverina, has been named NSW Exporter of the Year. Photo: Gundagai Lamb.

From Old Mates Pub in Manhattan to Blue by Alain Ducasse in Bangkok, Gundagai Lamb has taken Riverina lamb onto international menus and added another notch to its tally with the NSW Exporter of the Year title.

The title is the highest honour at the annual NSW Export Awards, which recognise the achievements and resilience of exporters across the state.

Gundagai Lamb chief executive Will Barton said the award marked how far the business had come since the family set out to take its lamb to the world.

“Six years ago, we decided to chase our dream of delivering consistently better lamb around the globe – and just six years later, that dream is on the menu in more than 30 countries,” he said.

The brand’s global push is the latest chapter in a family story rooted in Gundagai’s meat trade.

In 1919, Fred W Barton began a butcher’s apprenticeship in South Gundagai before going on to operate Barton’s Butchery in the town’s main street.

His sons, Tony and Bill, followed him into the meat trade, taking the family business from retail into processing.

In 1974, they built a small abattoir on the outskirts of South Gundagai and established Gundagai Meat Processors which processed about 5000 lambs a year in its early days.

The company now says it processes around one million lambs annually.

A major step in that growth came in 2016, when Will led a $30 million expansion.

The project not only secured Tier 2 export status for the plant, giving the company access to overseas markets including the United States, it also created 76 full-time jobs.

Gundagai Lamb launched in 2020, with its proprietary GLQ grading score introduced two years later.

The score uses measurements of each carcase’s marbling and lean meat yield, along with records of diseases and defects found during processing.

“Using our world-first objective measurement technology, we measure flavour, tenderness and balance of every lamb at the point of processing,” Will said.

He said the grading was designed to give customers a more consistent eating experience and farmers detailed feedback about their flocks.

“The Riverina has produced exceptional lamb for generations, but the difference is that we’ve built a system to not just prove it, but consistently deliver it,” he said.

While the brand had also reached fine-dining restaurants in London and Tokyo, Hong Kong, Singapore, Macau, Japan, Saudi Arabia and, more recently, Malaysia, demand in the United States had increased ninefold over the past three financial years.

Gundagai Lamb chief executive Will Barton says the brand is now served in more than 30 countries. Photo: Gundagai Lamb.

In New York, Gundagai lamb is turning up in two very different settings: Yemenat, a Yemeni restaurant in Brooklyn listed in the Michelin Guide, and Old Mates Pub, an Australian pub in downtown Manhattan.

Yemenat’s menu includes lamb haneeth, a braised lamb shoulder dish, and lamb sughar, while at Old Mates, head chef Simon Drolz-Cox has served Gundagai lamb strip loin with herb sauce and marinated peppers.

BOA Steakhouse is an upscale American steakhouse brand with locations in California, Las Vegas and Austin.

Its West Hollywood menu lists Gundagai lamb lollipops with spiced labneh and pomegranate molasses.

In Bangkok, one-Michelin-starred Blue by Alain Ducasse featured Gundagai lamb at a special wine-pairing dinner in March. The lamb was cured in fig leaves and served with marsh samphire, morels and asparagus.

Red Sky, a rooftop restaurant on the 55th floor of Bangkok’s Centara Grand, also lists Gundagai lamb chops and fillet among its signature dishes.

The lamb appears on Australian menus, too, including one close to home.

Three Blue Ducks at Nimbo Fork, between Gundagai and Tumut in the Snowy Valleys, lists Gundagai lamb with chimichurri, carrots and peas.

In Sydney, two-hatted Atelier by Sofitel has roasted Gundagai lamb loin with zucchini flower on its spring menu.

Gundagai Lamb employs 350 people across its business, while about 250 family farming businesses supply lamb to the brand each year.

Will said the UK trade deal and the recently concluded EU agreement could open further opportunities.

He described the EU as, “a strong economy with a strong track record of consuming lamb”.

The company is also assessing opportunities in China and Japan.

Gundagai Lamb won both NSW Exporter of the Year and the Agribusiness, Food and Beverages category at the NSW Export Awards ceremony in Sydney on 28 October.

The category win puts the company in the running for the national Agribusiness, Food and Beverages Award.

The Australian Export Awards will be presented at Parliament House in Canberra on 18 November.

“Winning this award is not only an incredible token of recognition for all we have achieved, but it also unlocks new connections and opportunities to further our reach around the globe,” Will said.

“It is a credit to our producers, our team, our distributors and all those who keep coming back for more.”

Original Article published by Edwina Mason on About Regional.

australia.title: ‘It’s an architect’s dream’: five beautiful eco buildings around the world
australia.snippet: From a bamboo gym in Bali to a house made from earth in Wiltshire, these projects show the beauty in sustainable design With construction...
australia.content:
With construction accounting for more than a third of global emissions, sustainable architecture is central to the world meeting its climate targets. The following five creations from around the world exemplify how “green” buildings can also be beautiful.

Children’s Village, Tocantins, Brazil

In Tocantins, central Brazil, the Canuanã school is a boarding school whose pupils come from remote farming communities across the region. In 2017, architects gave the school’s 540 boarders two new “villages” of dormitories, one for girls and one for boys.

The buildings are made from locally sourced timber and earth bricks. A vast canopy shades the complex, and perforated brick walls let air pass through, so the bedrooms stay comfortable without air conditioning even when temperatures reach 45C. Under the roof, rooms open on to shady, landscaped courtyards and airy verandas.

David Mikhail, the co-founder of Mikhail Riches, a UK practice specialising in sustainable design, says: “It is absolutely fantastic. So beautiful. It does a lot with little resource, which is the essence of a sustainable approach.” He adds: “I love the economy of it, and the huge sense of place they managed to evoke through such elegant and limited means.”

The architects have said their biggest challenge was convincing pupils and teachers that earth, brick and timber could feel modern rather than old-fashioned. They managed to do so by listening to students through 10 days of workshops to understand what they wanted from the design.

The Arc, Bali, Indonesia

The Green school in Bali is surrounded by jungle and promotes sustainability through learning in a natural environment. Since it opened in 2008, it has been built almost entirely in bamboo. Its gymnasium, the Arc, was completed in 2021.

Inspired by a mammal’s ribcage, the Arc’s bamboo arches span a 760 sq metre sports court without a single column interrupting the floor space. The arches support an undulating canopy, and natural ventilation comes from breezes that flow in at the base, while warm air escapes through vents at the top.

Bamboo is a highly sustainable building material because of how quickly it can regrow; large varieties reach building strength in just three to six years. “It is so fast-growing and sequesters a lot of carbon dioxide very quickly, so using it for building is a bit of a no-brainer if you can make it work,” says Mikhail. “And not only have they made it work, they’ve done it absolutely beautifully.”

Sara Kulturhus, Skellefteå, Sweden

Skellefteå, a small city just south of the Arctic Circle, is surrounded by 480,000 hectares (1.2m acres) of forest, and features wooden schools, a wooden road bridge, even a wooden multistorey car park. In 2021 it added Sara Kulturhus, a 20-storey cultural centre and hotel that is one of the tallest timber buildings in the world. It houses two theatres, a museum, an art gallery, the city library and a hotel.

The building is made of glulam – layers of timber glued together – and cross-laminated timber, a kind of super-sized plywood. The hotel rooms arrived as prefabricated wooden pods and were stacked into place. Building in wood saved a year in construction time compared with steel and concrete, while the timber came from trees harvested within 40 miles of the site, and replacement trees have since been planted.

“It promotes a love affair with wood and timber, and the localism of that in an area like Sweden is fabulous,” Mikhail says. “The lovely thing about cross-laminated timber is that the trees you use to make the panels don’t have to be elderly specimen trees. They can be relatively fast-grown and sustainably farmed.”

The Forest, Hobart, Australia

When the University of Tasmania was planning the redevelopment of its main campus in central Hobart, the architects chose to adapt what was already there rather than demolish it and start again. Two early 20th-century brick warehouses and a heritage-listed glass dome were stitched together into a single campus of classrooms and study spaces, which opened in February 2026.

At its heart is the glass dome, built in 1997. It is filled with about 3,200 native plants, including various species of ferns, and has an integrated watering, misting and fogging system that recreates rainforest-like growing conditions.

“You could argue the most sustainable building is actually no building, and the second most sustainable building is a refurbished old building,” says Mikhail. “That’s what this is: they’re taking existing structures and breathing new life into them, reimagining what they could be.”

Rammed Earth House, Cranborne Chase, UK

On the site of a former brickworks in the Wiltshire countryside, this house has been built from the ground beneath it. Rammed earth, which has been used since the Neolithic period, is a building material made of soil that has been compacted layer by layer into thick walls. Here, clay-rich soil was dug up and mixed with rubble from demolished outbuildings and local limestone.

The earth is “unstabilised”, meaning no cement has been added, which makes this one of only a few UK buildings made that way. Unstabilised earth could, in principle, simply go back into the ground if the house were ever demolished.

Rammed earth’s thermal mass also evens out temperature and moisture indoors, which the architects say will matter more as the climate warms. “As a piece of architecture, I think it’s phenomenal,” says Mikhail. “It’s an architect’s dream, and I’m slightly envious of it, I’ll be honest.”

“It’s like a beautiful piece of jewellery, and it riffs on lots of really lovely sustainable ideas.”

australia.title: Microsoft ‘deeply sorry’ for global outage that could have billion-dollar impact on Australia
australia.snippet: Experts say disruption exposes ‘Australia’s reliance on foreign technology’ as software giant says services being restored Get our breaki...
australia.content:
The Microsoft outage could be a disaster for the Australian economy that forces some small businesses to close, with costs expected to run into the billions of dollars, experts have warned.

The US software company has said it is “deeply sorry” for a widespread outage that caused disruption to millions of users, organisations and businesses across the globe – and that it has “addressed the underlying issue”.

The company said the outage was a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents, and that it continued to gradually restore services.

Experts have said the outage exposes “Australia’s reliance on foreign technology” and that people unable to be paid, send an invoice, or access government services “are entitled to be worried”.

The outage of Microsoft’s services, which began on Friday morning, lasted roughly 18 hours before services started to recover. Microsoft said it was bringing back services gradually to ensure a stable restoration.

Ashwin Pal, a partner at the risk advisory firm RSM Australia, said his clients had activated business continuity and disaster recovery plans, but many businesses didn’t have a fallback.

“A protracted event like this can easily be the straw that breaks the camel’s back for smaller entities,” Pal said.

Pal said Microsoft had obviously struggled to recover, which raised bigger questions.

“I’m a technologist and I’m actually flabbergasted as to how something like this could have happened … they pushed out a change which should have been tested,” Pal said.

The Australian Computer Society has renewed calls for the federal government to urgently review which critical IT systems rely on a single provider, and where backup options could keep the economy running.

The society’s chief executive, Prins Ralston, said the outage had “exposed Australia’s reliance on foreign technology”, particularly on small businesses.

“Australians who couldn’t get paid, couldn’t send an invoice, or couldn’t reach a government service this morning are entitled to be worried,” Ralston said.

Australian hospitals and health clinics were affected by the outage, although the Australian Medical Association (AMA) on Friday said had been no impacts for patient care.

“We’ve had some facilities return to using paper for scripts because authentication to get into lots of prescribing software requires multifactor verification, which requires you to be able to access your Microsoft-supported email,” said the AMA’s president, Dr Michael Bonning.

Courts in South Australia and Victoria reported that the outage had affeced its email system. Many schools across the country were also affected.

Service NSW, the one-stop shop agency for residents, drivers, and business owners to access government services, encouraged customers to delay their visits to its service centres.

Federal government departments have also been maffectedy the outage, including national security agencies.

The head the domestic spy agency Asio, Mike Burgess, on Friday said the organisation’s systems “operate on multiple levels”, adding that they had been affected “on one level, yes, but not completely”.

The outage has affected businesses and organisations across the world that use Microsoft products.

In the UK, healthcare systems were disrupted and several British police forces urged people not to try to report crimes online and to phone them in instead.

US government offices across the country have been affected by the outage, including congressional offices that heavily rely on Outlook email. The US House’s chief administrative officer that handles IT for the chamber sent out a “campus-wide alert” to staffers on Thursday about the outage, Politico reported.

In Japan, the shipping company Sagawa Express said it was unable to accept online reservations for some of its services at airports and train stations while Taisho, a leading pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone.

When stock market trading opened on Wall Street, shares in Microsoft dipped slightly, down 1.1% at $516.86.

Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by problems with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running.

Microsoft’s executive vice-president of Copilot, Charles Lamanna, said: “We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue.”

australia.title: US-bound flights out of Australia delayed after telecommunications outage grounded American planes
australia.snippet: Sydney and Melbourne airports say flights were affected by now-lifted ban on departures in US US flight outage – live updates Get our bre...
australia.content:
Some US-bound flights from Sydney airport were grounded or delayed on Saturday after American authorities halted departures and delayed landings at all US airports.

Flights from Melbourne airport were also affected, with travel for passengers expected to depart for Los Angeles shortly after 10am being delayed by almost three hours.

Sydney airport confirmed the US ban on flight arrivals was lifted shortly before 1pm, although it was not known how this would impact delays.

Earlier, the airport confirmed some US-bound flights had been grounded.

“We are aware of the nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration and are monitoring the situation closely,” the spokesperson said.

“Passengers travelling to or via the United States should check with their airline for the latest information regarding their flight.”

Passengers on US bound flights from Sydney Airport reported being stuck on the tarmac for three hours before eventually departing. One plane required extra fuel after running air-conditioning for several hours while waiting.

The FAA announced the nationwide pause in response to “a temporary telecommunications outage”. It has since lifted the grounding order, as it continued to investigate the cause of the outage.

Passengers on two US-bound flights from Melbourne airport, which were due to depart at 12pm and 12.45pm, were also delayed due to the situation in the US.

A flight to Dallas, scheduled for 10am, departed at around 1pm, shortly after the US ban was lifted.

By 3pm Saturday, all delayed flights from Melbourne had departed.

Qantas thanked passengers for their patience and recommended people with upcoming flights to the US to check its website for more information.

Four flights from Brisbane were also delayed.. Two had departed by 3pm on Saturday.

“Passengers travelling to North America are advised to contact their airline for the latest information about their flight,” a Brisbane Airport spokesperson said.

australia.title: Hundreds take to water for Newcastle coal port protest despite attempt by NSW police to stop them
australia.snippet: About 600 Rising Tide activists were in the water at Newcastle port, with hundreds more onshore Get our breaking news email , free app or...
australia.content:
A climate group has overcome efforts by police and the New South Wales government to stop a protest at the world’s largest coal port, with hundreds of people taking to the water to unfurl a sign that said “coal exports = climate chaos”.

About 600 Rising Tide protesters paddled on kayaks and water crafts into the Port of Newcastle on Saturday to demand funding for coal workers to transition to new jobs and a safe and livable climate. Hundreds more protested onshore, after an 11th-hour victory in the supreme court enabled the Paddle for the Planet event to proceed.

No arrests were made during Saturday’s action.

Rising Tide’s spokesperson, Joe Hallenstein, said the protest aimed to “call out” the lack of climate action by Anthony Albanese and the state’s premier, Chris Minns.

“As hypocritical Albo parades around Cop31 urging world leaders to take stronger climate action, back home he and his Labor counterpart, premier Chris Minns, are approving new coal and gas projects and attempting to silence us.”

It followed an uncertain week, after the Newcastle city council – in consultation with Minns and the police minister, Yasmin Catley – banned Rising Tide and any affiliated groups from using council-owned land to undertake any protests.

Minns wrote to the council ahead of the motion for the ban on Tuesday night, saying it was “not possible for the council to distance itself from the illegal activities that occur at these protests”. Meanwhile Catley labelled Rising Tide “bad faith actors” after they defied police directions during 2024 and 2025 protests, resulting in mass arrests.

The protest did not use council-owned land, so was not subject to the ban. The group applied to police for what is known as a form 1, a permit-style system that protest organisers have the option of submitting to prevent participants from being charged under the summary offences act.

The group submitted the form 1 to police two months in advance, despite only being required to give seven days’ notice. The police took six weeks to notify organisers that they would not agree to the form 1, leading to a supreme court hearing this week to settle the dispute.

On Friday, justice Edward Muston sided with the protesters. He acknowledged the safety risks, but said Rising Tide had mitigated those risks.

“I have accepted that the possibility of participants engaging in actions which lie outside the parameters of the proposed public assembly cannot be excluded,” Muston said. “However, I was not satisfied that the making of orders of the type sought by the commissioner [of police] would reduce in any material way the likelihood of such actions occurring.”

“Ultimately, I found that in balancing the considerations, the public interest in the facilitation of political expression through assembly outweighs the legitimate concerns which have been expressed by the [police] commissioner.”

The group will hold its annual six-day festival in Newcastle, one of the biggest climate protests in Australia, in February. It remains to be seen how the ban on the use of council land will impact its activities.

The event draws attention to its demands for the cancellation of all new fossil fuel projects, an end to coal exports from Newcastle by 2030, and taxing fossil fuel profits at 78% to fund community and industrial transitions.

During the 2024 protest, the Minns government attempted to stop the event from going ahead by establishing a maritime exclusion zone around the port. But just as the protest was kicking off, the supreme court found the government had acted improperly and ruled the exclusion zone invalid.

During the event 173 protesters were charged, but charges against 125 of those people were withdrawn in August.

At the 2025 blockade, police arrested and charged 129 protesters who entered the water, preventing three coal ships from entering the port. They remain before the courts.

australia.title: Stuart Bonds made ‘racist’ and ‘divisive’ comments. But One Nation is showing no sign of dumping the NSW candidate
australia.snippet: The former coalminer’s claim Australians are being ‘demographically replaced’ sparked wide criticism, but his party has shown no signs of...
australia.content:
In a Facebook video from a Sydney anti-immigration rally on Sunday, as a man dressed like a medieval knight watches on, One Nation’s lead upper house candidate, Stuart Bonds, launches into a speech against “mass” migration.

“Make no mistake, we are being demographically replaced inside our own nation,” he says.

“If we don’t support Australian mothers having Australian children, we [are] going to pay for other cultures’ children to be brought up in our lands.”

In an apparent allusion to the “great replacement theory”, a far-right conspiracy theory that white westerners are being actively “replaced” by minority ethnic immigrants, he continued: “That’s the socialist plan, is to destroy and bring down and tear down the fabric of your civilisation.”

The comments sparked a wave of criticism, but the party has shown no signs of taking Bonds off the ticket for the 2027 New South Wales state election. One Nation did, however, dump one candidate this week: the Victorian branch disendorsed a lower-house candidate over an old social media post describing Hitler as the “GOAT”, an acronym for greatest of all time.

The rally was not a one-off. On a podcast released on Monday with the rally’s organiser, the Australian Lobby Group, Bonds appeared to double down on the remarks. He did not challenge host Scott Challen’s assertion that Labor governments were building “ethnic voting blocks with Middle Eastern and subcontinent people … to stack the numbers to entrench power for themselves”, instead responding: “Mate, and that’s why we’re going to get rid of all of the multicultural grants, right?”

On Wednesday, in an interview with ABC Upper Hunter, Bonds responded to questions about his comments by citing Australian Bureau of Statistics data that shows the proportion of Australians born overseas has trended upward since the end of the second world war, from 10% in 1945 to 32% in 2025. He did not mention that the proportion of Australians born overseas was at its highest – 32.4% – in 1891, the first year of available data.

Bonds said with the Australian birthrate beneath the 2.1 required to replace the population, “I would just like to know what people assume is going to happen.”

“Where are these people going to come from?” he said.

NSW Labor pounced on the rally comments immediately, with the state’s premier, Chris Minns, calling them “frankly outrageous and racist”. The government passed motions in both houses censuring Bonds, not yet a member.

The Coalition followed four days later. On Wednesday afternoon, the opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said Bonds’ language was “clearly divisive”.

But she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement with One Nation after the March state election.

“We will not form a coalition with One Nation, [but] we’ll work with anyone post-election if we’re in a minority government,” she told reporters.

The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the party to go into a Coalition with One Nation. And with the Coalition consistently polling behind One Nation, that makes Bonds not a fringe candidate, but a potentially influential figure.

One Nation could ‘clean the deck’ in regions

The ABC’s former election analyst, Antony Green, said the remarks played straight into Labor’s hands.

“This will certainly be something the Labor party uses in all those multi-ethnic seats in Sydney,” he said – seats like those on the rural fringes of Sydney, which One Nation said it plans to target.

Indeed the deputy premier, Prue Car, who has Indian heritage and whose electorate of Londonderry is one of the seats in question, gave an impassioned critique of Bonds’ comments in question time on Tuesday.

“Who’s he [Bonds] talking about when he talks about this?” she said. “I tell you who he’s talking about – he’s talking about families like mine, and families that I represent.”

Kos Samaras, a former Labor strategist who is now a director of polling group Redbridge, said that while the comments likely won’t play well in Sydney seats – including alienating moderate Liberal voters worried about the party going into Coalition with One Nation – “you might be able to get away with it in certain parts of NSW”.

And Bonds, a former coalminer, has made his base in the Hunter.

Samaras said One Nation could “clean the deck” in the regions, including Labor-held seats in the Hunter, and “pretty much anything else the Coalition hasn’t got bolted down to the ground”.

The NSW One Nation leader, Mike Newman, who in September said he “made a mistake” when he told a Sydney rally he wanted to stop abortions, did not respond directly when asked if he agreed with Bonds’ comments or if he would rein in his first-placed upper house candidate.

“What I will say is that what Stuart Bonds is a patriotic Aussie. He’s a coalminer. He has very, very strong views,” he said on Tuesday.

Newman, who previously rejected claims that One Nation was racist, said on Tuesday: “What we want to do is … protect Australian values, and that is the fundamental thing that Stuart Bonds is pushing for. It’s about assimilation.”

The NSW treasurer, Daniel Mookhey, whose parents immigrated to Australia from India in the 1970s, told the ABC that Bonds’ comments were not grounded in reality.

“I think he’s saying that there is a deliberate conspiracy to use migrants to replace the way he puts it, native-born Australians for political reasons,” Mookhey said.

The quota for election to the upper house is 4.5%, making Bonds all but guaranteed to be elected, with One Nation polling in the high 20s and low 30s in recent months.

Green expects the party to pick up four or five seats in the upper house; so far it has only named three candidates: Newman, Bonds and Jeff Bacon, a firearms manufacturer who is second on the upper house ticket.

But unlike Victoria, NSW has optional preferential voting, which means when that state goes to the polls in March, lower house preference flows aren’t guaranteed.

But Bonds has downplayed whether he may have jeopardised a future preference deal with the Coalition.

“If the Coalition have a problem with facts, the same as the Labor party, then maybe it will,” he told the ABC.

“But I’m not here to impress the Coalition.”

world.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
world.snippet: After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-...
world.content:
The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.

Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.

The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”

She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.

“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”

Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.

Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.

Associated Press contributed to this report

world.title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
world.snippet: Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent Lewis Hamilton has visited Egyp...
world.content:
Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.

The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.

“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.

A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.

Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.

Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.

At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.

Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.

The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.

The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

world.title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
world.snippet: President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo Seven people were killed and...
world.content:
Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.

The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.

An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.

The health ministry gave the casualty toll, adding more than 70 of the injured were discharged after receiving treatment.

Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways.

Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.

Gamal said he saw about 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to hospital. Some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and died, he said.

Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation.

Outside al-Wasta central hospital in Beni Suef province, where some of the injured were taken for treatment, survivors said passengers were in shock and struggling to breathe because of all the dust that was kicked up. Nearby villagers eventually got them out, they said.

Farha Gamal, a survivor who was inside the Fayyoum train, said she saw some of the passengers who appeared dead and others were struggling to find their way out of the car. “There were other cars that were completely mangled,” she said in an interview.

Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the crash site to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.

Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.

Egypt’s deadliest train crash was in 2002 when more than 300 people were killed after a fire broke out on an overnight train journeying from Cairo to southern Egypt.

world.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
world.snippet: See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and...
world.content:
African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.

See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.

The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.

See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.

Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.

While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.

Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.

“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.

“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”

Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.

As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.

Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.

“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.

“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”

See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

world.title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children
world.snippet: Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families The l...
world.content:
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran ​a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.

His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.

In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.

Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.

The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.

It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.

In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.

The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.

Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.

Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.

The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in March 2023, when a man told ​police his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police rearrested him and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.

Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.

Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.

Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

Reuters contributed reporting
